title: Integration by Substitution
summary: Substitution reverses the chain rule: let $u=g(x)$ so $du=g'(x)\,dx$, converting $\int f(g(x))g'(x)\,dx$ into $\int f(u)\,du$. It handles composites, and with $u=\ln$ or exponentials, integrals like $\int\frac{g'}{g}\,dx=\ln|g|+C$.

u-substitution.plain: Renaming an inner expression $u$ to simplify an integral.
u-substitution.in_class: Reverses the chain rule: $\int f(g)g'\,dx=\int f(u)\,du$.

differential du.in_class: Match it to a factor of the integrand.

inner function.in_class: Usually inside a power, root, trig, or exponential.

change of limits.in_class: Then you never convert back to $x$.

back-substitute.plain: Replacing $u$ with $g(x)$ at the end (indefinite integrals).
back-substitute.in_class: Not needed if you changed the limits.

adjust constants.in_class: e.g. supply a missing factor of $\tfrac12$.

concept_sections.heading: The idea
concept_sections.explanation: Substitution undoes the chain rule. Spot an inner function $g(x)$ whose derivative $g'(x)$ also appears (up to a constant). Let $u=g(x)$, $du=g'(x)\,dx$, and rewrite everything in $u$.

concept_sections.heading: Adjusting constants
concept_sections.explanation: If $du$ is off by a constant factor, multiply and divide to fix it. For $\int x e^{x^2}\,dx$, $u=x^2$ gives $du=2x\,dx$, so supply a $\tfrac12$.
math_steps: Insert the reciprocal constant to match.

concept_sections.heading: Definite integrals: change the limits
concept_sections.explanation: For $\int_a^b$, convert the $x$-limits to $u$-limits with $u=g(x)$ and integrate in $u$ — no need to switch back to $x$.
math_steps: Integrate in $u$ over the new limits.

concept_sections.heading: The logarithm pattern
concept_sections.explanation: When the numerator is the derivative of the denominator, $\int\dfrac{g'(x)}{g(x)}\,dx=\ln|g(x)|+C$ — substitution with $u=g$.
math_steps: Check: is the top the derivative of the bottom?

concept_sections.heading: Exponentials and trig via substitution
concept_sections.explanation: Integrals like $\int e^{g}g'\,dx=e^{g}+C$ and $\int\cos(g)g'\,dx=\sin(g)+C$ are direct substitutions with $u=g$.

real_world_examples.title: Cooling that depends on temperature
real_world_examples.scenario: A model's rate depends on the current state.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Separating and integrating yields $\int\frac{du}{u}=\ln|u|$ — the log pattern from substitution.

real_world_examples.title: Work with a variable force
real_world_examples.scenario: Force changes as an object moves.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Integrating $F(x)\,dx$ over a composite path often calls for a substitution to simplify the inner dependence.

real_world_examples.title: Chain-rule in reverse for signals
real_world_examples.scenario: A waveform is a function of a phase that varies.
real_world_examples.how_the_math_applies: Integrating $\cos(\text{phase})\cdot(\text{phase})'$ uses substitution to recover the amplitude.
